title: Why do some heavy things float?
outcome: The student will explain that floating depends on density (mass per unit volume) compared to water, not just weight.
subject: physics

concepts.title: Why do some heavy things float?
concepts.centralCause: An object floats if its average density is less than the density of water (1 g/cm3) and sinks if it is greater.
conditions: The body is uniform and has no hidden cavities (unless specified)
The body does not soak up water or dissolve
The body is in ordinary fresh water
The body is not held by any external force

cards.title: Weight vs. Density

fact.statement: Whether an object sinks depends on its density, which is how much mass is packed into a specific volume.
conditions: The body is in still water
fact.source: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure; 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY 4.0) — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: Can a giant ship made of heavy steel float while a tiny pebble sinks?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict what happens if we keep the material the same but change the size. Tell me why.

cards.explanation: Density is a measure of how 'crowded' the atoms are inside an object. It is calculated by dividing mass by volume. A heavy object might float if it takes up a huge amount of space, making its density lower than water.

action.instruction: Imagine a large block of wood and a small piece of wood. If you keep the material the same but change the size, does the smaller piece sink?
constants: The liquid it is placed in

question.prompt: If you have a huge piece of cork and a small piece of cork, which one will float? Explain why.

key.expectedCause: Both will float because they are made of the same material with the same density.
acceptable: Both float because cork is less dense than water
key.typicalMistake: The big one floats because it is bigger.
key.followUp: Does the size of the object change its density if the material stays the same?

cards.title: The Rule of 1 g/cm3

fact.statement: Water has a density of 1 g/cm3. Objects with a density higher than 1 g/cm3 sink.
fact.source: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure; 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY 4.0) — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: Why does a stone sink but a piece of wood floats?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict which will sink if we know the stone's density is 2 g/cm3. Explain your reasoning.

cards.explanation: To see if something floats, we compare it to water. If an object's density is greater than 1 g/cm3, it is 'heavier' for its size than water is, so it sinks. If it is less, it floats.

action.instruction: Think of a stone with a density of 2 g/cm3 and a piece of wood with a density of 0.6 g/cm3. Predict which sinks.

cards.title: Cutting the Stone

fact.statement: Cutting a uniform object in half keeps its density the same.
conditions: The body does not soak up water
fact.source: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure; 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY 4.0) — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: If you cut a sinking stone in half, will the halves still sink?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict what happens to the sinking behavior of the halves. Explain why.

cards.explanation: Density is a property of the material. When you cut an object, you reduce its mass and its volume by the same proportion. Because both mass and volume change together, the density stays the same.

action.instruction: Imagine a stone that sinks. If you cut it in half, does the density change?

cards.title: The Secret of the Ship

fact.statement: Hollow bodies float because the air inside lowers their average density.
conditions: The body does not soak up water
fact.source: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure; 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY 4.0) — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: How can a massive steel ship float while a small piece of steel sinks?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict what happens if the ship's hull fills with water. Explain why.

cards.explanation: A ship is hollow. When we calculate its average density, we include the air inside. Because the air is very light, the average density of the whole ship becomes less than the density of water.

action.instruction: Imagine a hollow plastic bottle. If you fill it with water, does its average density change?

worlds.scene: A pirate ship floats on a magical sea because of the air trapped in its hull.
worlds.illustration: A pirate ship on the ocean.

question.prompt: Why does a hollow steel ship float? What would happen if the hull filled with water?

key.expectedCause: It floats because the air makes the average density lower than water. If it fills with water, the average density rises and it sinks.
acceptable: The air makes it less dense. If it fills with water, it becomes denser than water and sinks.
key.typicalMistake: It floats because it is big.
key.followUp: Does the weight of the ship change when it fills with water?

criteria.example: The air makes the average density lower than water.

fact.statement: To predict if an object floats, calculate its density (mass/volume) and compare it to 1 g/cm3.
conditions: The body does not soak up water
fact.source: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure; 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY 4.0) — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: Can you predict which objects will float without seeing them?
hook.predictPrompt: Predict which objects will float and explain your reasoning for each.

cards.explanation: To solve any floating problem, find the density. Divide the mass by the volume. If the result is less than 1 g/cm3, it floats. If it is more, it sinks.

question.prompt: Object A has a mass of 400 g and a volume of 500 cm3. Object B has a mass of 150 g and a volume of 100 cm3. Which one floats and why?

key.expectedCause: Object A floats because its density is 0.8 g/cm3 (less than 1). Object B sinks because its density is 1.5 g/cm3 (greater than 1).
